Title: proposal: unsafe: add Transmute generic function for convenient type reinterpretation

Body: ### Proposal Details

### Summary

Propose adding a generic `unsafe.TransmuteT, F any T` function to the unsafe package for convenient type reinterpretation.

### Background & Motivation

Currently, performing type casting or memory reinterpretation via unsafe requires verbose and error-prone pointer conversions and dereferences:

 [CODE_BLOCK] // Current approach
_ = *(*float32)(unsafe.Pointer(&value))
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Similar to how unsafe.SliceData and unsafe.StringData were introduced in Go 1.20 to simplify common unsafe pointer operations and improve ergonomics, a dedicated helper function like unsafe.Transmute would make intentional memory reinterpretation cleaner and easier to read.

This would significantly reduce boilerplate and improve ergonomics for authors of high-performance libraries (such as ECS frameworks, custom serializers, and custom collection types). Instead of forcing library authors to write unsafe pointer acrobatics, unsafe.Transmute provides a clean, standard, and self-documenting primitive for working with generic memory layouts.

Even low-level code should be simple, clear, and readable. Code is read far more often than it is written, and replacing syntactic pointer gymnastics with an explicit function makes the developer's intent crystal clear.

### Proposed API

 [CODE_BLOCK] package unsafe

// Transmute reinterprets the memory of value as type T.
func TransmuteT, F any (to T)
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### Use Case

In low-level systems, components are often stored in untyped or raw memory buffers.

 [CODE_BLOCK] // Before
value := *(*T)(unsafe.Pointer(&raw))

// After
value := unsafe.TransmuteT
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### Alternatives Considered

Keeping the explicit `*(*T)(unsafe.Pointer(&value))` pattern. However, explicit generic primitives in `unsafe` significantly improve readability and reduce syntax clutter.

Title: Agent host sessions can show as non-archived despite server-archived state

Body: Agent host sessions have server-authoritative archived state (the `SessionStatus.IsArchived` bit, surfaced as `IChatSessionItem.archived`). However, `AgentSessionsModel.isArchived()` merges that provider value with a locally-persisted view-state overlay and gives the **local** overlay precedence:

 [CODE_BLOCK] private isArchived(session: IInternalAgentSessionData): boolean {
 return this.resolveStateEntry(session)?.archived ?? Boolean(session.archived);
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Because `??` only falls through on `null`/`undefined`, a persisted local entry with `archived: false` (e.g. from a prior local unarchive) permanently masks the server's `archived: true`. The result: a session the server reports as archived (e.g. an errored + archived session with status `66` = `Error | IsArchived`) stays in the non-archived date sections and never lands in the Archived section.

### Fix

For agent host sessions, ignore the local view-state overlay and use only the server-backed `session.archived`. Non-agent-host providers keep the existing overlay behavior.

### Note / follow-up

The chat sessions viewer's own Archive/Unarchive actions only write the local model state (`session.setArchived(...)`); the `IChatSessionItemController` has no archive method, so they never dispatch to the agent host. With this fix, those local writes no longer affect an agent-host session's displayed archived state — only the Agents window path (`baseAgentHostSessionsProvider.archiveSession`) dispatches `SessionIsArchivedChanged` to the server. If those viewer buttons should work for agent-host sessions, they need to be routed to the server separately.

Title: os,internal/poll: reads from closed pipes sometimes do not unblock on darwin

Body: ```
#!watchflakes
post <- goos == "darwin" && log ~ `os/exec\.\(\*Cmd\)\.awaitGoroutines` && log ~ `internal/poll\.\(\*pollDesc\)\.waitRead` &&
 !(builder ~ `(gotip|go1\.\d\d)-` && date < "2024-01-18")
```

We have been tracking a long-running bug on macOS (`darwin`) in [URL] That issue title doesn't accurately capture the widespread nature of the problem, nor its defining symptom or suspected root cause; so, I am filing a new issue for it.

On macOS, we see a pattern of test failures with the following characteristics:
- A goroutine is blocked on a `read` operation on a pipe.
- The pipe is known to be closed, because the process on the other end has either terminated (most often) or explicitly closed the pipe (less frequent, but sometimes seen in cases like #57369).

Many of these bugs have been worked around by explicitly canceling (or adding a timeout to) the stuck read.

The issues with this symptom have included:
- #60099
- #54461
- #61073
- #61128

A few other issues may be related but don't (or didn't) include goroutine dumps for the stuck process: they may or may not be due to this failure mode.
- #56231
- #57369
- #59657
- #61595
- #61779
- #63258
- #63731
- #64110
- #64269
- #64700
- #64959

Given the symptoms, it seems likely to me that this is either a bug in `internal/poll`, or a bug in the macOS platform that we have somehow started to trigger.

Title: x/crypto/acme: invalid Retry-After values can stop retries or cause tight polling

Body: The x/crypto/acme package does not safely handle malformed or expired Retry-After header values.

A negative delay-seconds value such as:

 Retry-After: -1

is accepted by strconv.Atoi and converted to a negative duration. In the default retry path, adding the existing jitter still produces a non-positive duration, causing the retry loop to stop with "no more retries".

An expired HTTP-date can also produce a negative duration. WaitOrder and WaitAuthorization only check for d == 0, so a negative duration is passed to time.NewTimer and causes immediate polling, potentially resulting in a tight request loop.

The default backoff path also indexes the header value directly. A response containing:

 http.Header{"Retry-After": nil}

can therefore panic.

Expected behavior:

- reject negative and overflowing delay-seconds values;
- ignore malformed and expired Retry-After values;
- fall back to the default backoff when the value is unusable;
- avoid indexing a possibly empty header slice.

### What did you do?

On Windows, a parent process starts two children that share an inherited, overlapped named-pipe handle as stdout. One child is a Go program; the other is a non-Go program that writes to the pipe with a synchronous WriteFile. The launcher here is OpenSSH Server, but anything that hands children an inherited overlapped pipe as stdout will do.

The Go program does nothing itself. A blank import of os is enough: os package initialization builds os.Stdout via `os.NewFile` before main runs. (Any import that pulls in os, e.g. fmt, triggers it too.)

`test.go`
 [CODE_BLOCK] package main
import (
 _ "os"
)
func main() {
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

`writefile.cpp`, a synchronous writer to STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE. It writes the same buffer twice. The payload is larger than the pipe buffer (0x1142 bytes > 4096) so each write takes the STATUS_PENDING path rather than completing inline:

 [CODE_BLOCK] #include 
#include 
char buffer[0x1142];
int main()
{
 DWORD dw;
 memset(buffer, 'X', sizeof(buffer)-2);
 buffer[sizeof(buffer)-2] = '\n';
 buffer[sizeof(buffer)-1] = 0;
 HANDLE h = GetStdHandle(STD_OUTPUT_HANDLE);
 // do this 2 times (hangs in the 2nd WriteFile())
 if (!WriteFile(h, buffer, sizeof(buffer), &dw, NULL)) {
 fprintf(stderr, "ERROR:WriteFile:%u\n", GetLastError());
 return 1;
 }
 fprintf(stderr, "INFO: 1st WriteFile() completed\n");
 if (!WriteFile(h, buffer, sizeof(buffer), &dw, NULL)) {
 fprintf(stderr, "ERROR:WriteFile:%u\n", GetLastError());
 return 1;
 }
 fprintf(stderr, "INFO: 2nd WriteFile() completed\n");
 return 0;
}

 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

`repro.bat` runs the Go program first (so os init associates the inherited stdout pipe with the runtime completion port), then the C writer on that same handle:

 [CODE_BLOCK] test.exe
writefile.exe

 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Save the three files to a local path (e.g. C:\repro\), build both (gcc writefile.cpp -o writefile.exe; go build test.go), then run them under the SSH server so they inherit the same overlapped stdout pipe. Use an absolute path; the sshd session's logon context resolves relative paths against its own home dir and may not see mapped network drives:

`ssh localhost C:\repro\repro.bat`

Note, OpenSSH Server has to be running locally. On a stock Windows box it ships as an optional feature and starts out stopped:

 [CODE_BLOCK] Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name OpenSSH.Server~~~~0.0.1.0 # if not already present
Start-Service sshd
Set-Service -Name sshd -StartupType Automatic

 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you see happen?

The sibling (non-Go) process's synchronous WriteFile never completes. It blocks in NtWaitForSingleObject inside WriteFile, waiting on a completion event that never fires. The Go process is the cause, not the victim; it does not itself hang. writefile.exe prints its first status line and hangs before the second:

 [CODE_BLOCK] INFO: 1st WriteFile() completed
 

 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Rebuilding only test.exe with an older toolchain, keeping the C writer and run steps identical, makes it go away, so the Go version is the only variable:

 | `test.exe` built with | 1st `WriteFile` | 2nd `WriteFile` | result |
 |---|---|---|---|
 | go1.24.6 | completes | completes | no hang |
 | go1.26.0 | completes | never returns | sibling hangs |

(Confirmed the toolchain baked into each binary with `go version -m test.exe.`)

This needs no special code to trigger. os initialization runs NewFile on the inherited stdout/stderr before main, so any Go binary that imports `os`, directly or transitively (e.g. via `fmt`), sets it off. Any launcher that shares an overlapped pipe across its children, such as a CI runner, build orchestrator, or SSH-based test harness, can end up with a non-Go process's writes silently hanging.

### What did you expect to see?

The sibling's synchronous WriteFile completes normally, as it does under go1.24 and earlier. `os.NewFile` on an inherited handle should adopt it passively and not change the completion behavior of a handle shared with another process.

### Analysis
The regression bisects to the overlapped-NewFile work in go1.25 (CL 662236, commit 7e60bdd, closing #19098). Under this change `os.NewFile` associates an inherited overlapped stdout/stderr pipe with the runtime's I/O completion handling before main runs. As part of this it calls the WINAPI `SetFileCompletionNotificationModes()` on the handle. That call alters the behavior of the underlying kernel file object, which is shared by every process that inherited the handle, not just the Go program's instance. After it runs, a sibling process's synchronous WriteFile on that same handle no longer completes. Removing that association for the inherited handle stops the hang.

This looks related to #76391 (NewFile blocking on a busy handle), but that is about a Go process's own I/O; here the Go process is fine and a separate process's write on a shared inherited handle hangs.

We have a local candidate fix that extends the existing Stdin exemption in os/file_windows.go to Stdout/Stderr:

 [CODE_BLOCK] // See go.dev/issue/75949 and go.dev/issue/76391.
if kind == kindNewFile && h != syscall.Stdin && h != syscall.Stdout && h != syscall.Stderr {
 nonBlocking, _ = windows.IsNonblock(h)
}

 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

It resolves the reproducer and passes our validation testing.

Title: x/crypto/chacha20poly1305: pure Go AVX2 vectorization using Go 1.27 archsimd

Body: Summary 
 This
proposal presents an optimization and modernisation path for
 golang.org/x/crypto/chacha20poly1305 
by replacing the legacy hand-written Plan 9 assembly
( chacha20_amd64.s ,
 poly1305_amd64.s )
with 100% Pure Go AVX2 vectorization powered by the native
 simd/archsimd 
package introduced in Go 1.27 ( GOEXPERIMENT=simd ). 
 
 

 
 Motivation 
 1. Eliminating Legacy Plan 9 Assembly 
 The
current production kernels in golang.org/x/crypto 
rely on hand-maintained Plan 9 assembly files written several years
ago. While fast, assembly implementations: 
 
• Cannot be inlined into caller loops by the Go compiler. 
 
• Impose function call prologue/epilogue overhead on small chunks. 
 
• Are difficult to audit, maintain, and fuzz across architectures. 
 2. Pure Go Safety and Inlining 
 With
Go 1.27's simd/archsimd 
intrinsics, double-block 256-bit AVX2 operations are written directly
in Go: 
 
• The Go SSA compiler manages register allocation globally. 
 
• Bounds check elimination (BCE) and inlining function seamlessly
across package boundaries. 
 3. Robust Runtime CPU Detection and
Cross-Platform Fallback 
 The
implementation features a dynamic runtime CPU feature check: 
 
• Uses archsimd.X86.AVX2() 
to dispatch vector instructions only when supported by the host CPU. 
 
• Automatically falls back to pure scalar Go on older hardware and
non-x86 architectures ( arm64 ,
 riscv64 ). 
 
 

 
 Reference Implementation & Open Source Proof
of Concept 
 A
complete, working reference implementation conforming strictly to the
RFC 8439 standard ( crypto/cipher.AEAD )
is publicly available and tested: 
 
• Repository: [URL] 
 
• Target Subpackage: 
[URL] 
 
 

 
 Correctness & Security Verification 
 
• RFC 8439 Compliance: Validated bit-exact against standard
IETF test vectors and C reference test suites. 
 
• Differential Fuzzing: Tested with over 960,000 randomized
executions ( go
test -fuzz ) against
 golang.org/x/crypto/chacha20poly1305 
with zero discrepancies. 
 
• Zero Allocations: Measured 0 B/op and 0 allocs/op 
on both Seal 
and Open 
operations across all payload sizes. 
 
• Memory Hygiene: Constant-time arithmetic and automatic
zeroing of internal buffers via native clear() .

linux/amd64)

+ GOEXPERIMENT=simd :

Title: x/net/webdav: fatal stack overflow parsing deeply nested XML — internal/xml fork never got the Decoder.Skip fix (CVE-2022-28131)

Body: # webdav/internal/xml: Decoder.Skip still recursive — fatal stack overflow from deeply nested XML in LOCK/PROPFIND/PROPPATCH

## Summary

`webdav/internal/xml` is a fork of `encoding/xml` frozen in 2015 (per its own README,
pending namespace-behavior changes that have long since landed). `Decoder.Skip()` still
recurses once per nested element:

 [CODE_BLOCK] // webdav/internal/xml/read.go:673
func (d *Decoder) Skip() error {
 for {
 tok, err := d.Token()
 ...
 case StartElement:
 if err := d.Skip(); err != nil { // recursion depth = XML nesting depth
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The standard library had this exact bug — fixed in Go 1.19 by making `Skip` iterative
(golang/go#53614, CVE-2022-28131) — but the fix was never backported to the fork. The
fork's commit history since 2015 is cosmetic only (gofmt, comments, `min` builtin).

## Impact

An unauthenticated HTTP request kills the whole server process:

- `LOCK` → `readLockInfo` (xml.go:54)
- `PROPFIND` → `readPropfind` (xml.go:180)
- `PROPPATCH` → `readProppatch` (xml.go:498)

Any element in the request body that matches no struct field goes through `Skip()`.
With ~20M nested elements (a ~140 MB body; no body-size limit is enforced by the
handler), the goroutine stack hits the 1 GB limit:

 [CODE_BLOCK] runtime: goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit
fatal error: stack overflow
 golang.org/x/net/webdav/internal/xml.(*Decoder).getc(...)
 ...
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

This is a **fatal runtime error**, not a panic — `recover()` and net/http's
per-connection panic handling cannot intercept it; the process dies. Measured: 15M
nesting survives, 20M crashes, in seconds.

Fuzzers can't catch this: x/net has no webdav fuzz targets, and govulncheck can't map
CVE-2022-28131 onto the fork because the module and symbol paths differ.

## Fix

Backport the standard library fix — track depth with a counter instead of recursing
(mirrors golang/go@8e11e7d). One-function change plus a regression test; happy to send
the PR (I have it ready, all webdav + internal/xml tests pass).

Note: I'm aware the package README scopes security issues to RCE and escaping `Dir`,
with crashes treated as ordinary bugs — filing as a security-relevant stdlib-lag bug
either way, since deployments embed this handler widely and the fix is trivial.
